title: Razaullah Is a Reminder of Pakistan’s Talent — Now the PCB Must Protect It
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
paragraphs: Pakistan cricket has found another fast bowler who makes people stop and watch. Razaullah Mashwani’s remarkable Test debut against England at Edgbaston was another reminder of something Pakistan has known for decades: this country does not suffer from a shortage of cricketing talent. It suffers far more from its inability to consistently manage that talent once it has been discovered. The real challenge for the Pakistan Cricket Board is therefore not finding the next Razaullah. It is making sure that he does not become another story of enormous promise interrupted by injury, poor planning or premature burnout.

At 21, Razaullah has already shown qualities that cannot easily be taught. He has genuine pace, confidence against international batters and, as his explosive 81 from No. 9 demonstrated, considerable natural ability with the bat as well. Pakistan should celebrate his arrival.
But celebration must come with caution.
Pakistan cricket has seen this movie before.

Ihsanullah emerged from the PSL bowling above 150 kilometres per hour and looked capable of becoming a major international fast bowler. Then came an elbow injury and a prolonged absence. More troublingly, the PCB’s own independent medical committee later identified delays in diagnosis, inappropriate treatment and the absence of the formal rehabilitation his condition required. The committee also acknowledged that Ihsanullah himself had not fully complied with rehabilitation protocols, but the institutional failures were serious enough to raise fundamental questions about how elite young athletes were being medically managed.
He is not an isolated example.

Naseem Shah was only 20 when a shoulder injury during the 2023 Asia Cup required surgery and ruled him out of the World Cup. Mohammad Hasnain suffered an ankle injury requiring extended rehabilitation. Mohammad Wasim Jr later underwent rehabilitation for a back injury. Arshad Iqbal and Zeeshan Zameer have also faced significant injury problems requiring specialist treatment.

Shaheen Shah Afridi’s injury history has similarly forced repeated discussion about workload and rest. The PCB itself has acknowledged the importance of rotation and workload management for fast bowlers, particularly after Pakistan entered major tournaments without key pacers fully available.

Not every injury can be blamed on the PCB. Fast bowling is physically demanding and injuries are an unavoidable part of professional sport. But when promising fast bowlers repeatedly suffer serious setbacks at young ages, the correct response is not simply to call it bad luck. The system has to ask whether workloads, rehabilitation, scheduling, medical supervision and selection decisions are good enough.
That is why Razaullah should not simply be encouraged to bowl faster.

Pakistan has a fascination with the speed gun. A young bowler reaches 145 km/h and immediately the question becomes whether he can reach 150. Yet longevity in international cricket comes from much more than pace.

Razaullah must be developed as a complete bowler: movement with the new ball, control with the old ball, variations, yorkers, tactical awareness and the ability to maintain effectiveness even when maximum pace is unnecessary.

His workload should also be monitored scientifically. Domestic cricket, Test matches, white-ball internationals, the PSL and overseas leagues cannot be treated as separate worlds. To a fast bowler’s body, an over is an over regardless of which shirt he is wearing.

The PCB should therefore prepare individual development programmes for its leading young fast bowlers, covering bowling loads, strength training, nutrition, recovery, injury prevention and planned rest.
And rest must stop being viewed as weakness.
Sometimes protecting a bowler from one tournament may preserve him for another five years.

Razaullah’s batting should also be developed rather than dismissed as a one-off performance. An 81 from No. 9 suggests natural lower-order ability. Pakistan does not need to turn him into a specialist batsman, but a fast bowler capable of contributing meaningful runs becomes considerably more valuable.
Above all, Pakistan needs a permanent national pace-development programme in which the PCB, domestic teams and PSL franchises share workload information, medical records and rehabilitation plans.
Pakistan has produced Shoaib Akhtar, Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis and generations of naturally gifted pacers. Even today, the supply of talent has not disappeared.
What remains uncertain is whether the system around that talent has evolved at the same pace.
Razaullah deserves applause for what he has achieved. But the greater responsibility now belongs to those managing him.
Pakistan already knows how to discover fast bowlers.
It must finally become equally good at keeping them fit, improving them patiently and allowing their talent to fulfil its promise.

title: انتخابی دیانت داری ہی پاکستان کے جمہوری مستقبل کا تعین کرے گی
imageAlt: Voters and the integrity of Pakistan’s elections
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
paragraphs: جمہوریت کا معیار صرف یہ نہیں کہ کتنے لوگ ووٹ ڈالنے نکلے، بلکہ اصل سوال یہ ہے کہ کیا عوام کو یقین ہے کہ ان کا ووٹ واقعی اہمیت رکھتا ہے۔ انتخابات کی قانونی حیثیت صرف آئین اور قانون کے مطابق انعقاد سے قائم نہیں ہوتی بلکہ اس اعتماد سے جنم لیتی ہے کہ انتخابی عمل آزاد، منصفانہ اور شفاف تھا۔ جب یہ اعتماد متزلزل ہوتا ہے تو جمہوریت بھی دباؤ کا شکار ہو جاتی ہے۔

ریکارڈو گونزالیز اور ان کے ساتھیوں کی ایک تقابلی تحقیق اسی حقیقت کی تصدیق کرتی ہے۔ اٹھارہ ممالک کے پینتیس ہزار سے زائد شہریوں پر کی گئی اس تحقیق سے معلوم ہوا کہ انتخابی بے ضابطگیوں کے بارے میں عوام کے ذاتی تجربات اور ان کے تاثرات، انتخابی اداروں کے رسمی ڈھانچے سے کہیں زیادہ ان کے جمہوریت پر اعتماد کو متاثر کرتے ہیں۔ دوسرے لفظوں میں، لوگ جمہوریت پر اپنا اعتماد اس بنیاد پر قائم نہیں کرتے کہ قانون کیا کہتا ہے، بلکہ اس بنیاد پر کرتے ہیں کہ وہ انتخابی عمل کے دوران کیا دیکھتے اور محسوس کرتے ہیں۔

یہ نتیجہ پاکستان کی انتخابی تاریخ سے بھی پوری طرح مطابقت رکھتا ہے۔ 2018ء اور 2024ء کے عام انتخابات، اگرچہ مختلف سیاسی حالات میں منعقد ہوئے، لیکن دونوں میں ایک بات مشترک رہی کہ انتخابی نتائج سے زیادہ بحث انتخابی شفافیت اور ساکھ پر ہونے لگی۔ انتخاب سے قبل کے ماحول، انتخابی مہم میں برابری، نتائج کے اعلان میں تاخیر، قانونی تنازعات اور انتخابی عمل کی شفافیت جیسے موضوعات قومی سیاسی بحث کا مرکز بنے رہے۔ ان اعتراضات کو مختلف سیاسی جماعتوں نے قبول کیا یا مسترد کیا، یہ اپنی جگہ اہم ہے، مگر اس سے بھی زیادہ اہم حقیقت یہ ہے کہ ان مباحث نے عوام کے ذہنوں میں انتخابات کی شفافیت کے بارے میں ایک مخصوص تاثر پیدا کیا۔

بین الاقوامی تحقیق بھی یہی بتاتی ہے کہ بعض اوقات عوامی تاثر خود حقیقت جتنی طاقت رکھتا ہے۔ اگر شہری یہ سمجھنے لگیں کہ انتخابات منصفانہ نہیں تھے تو جمہوریت سے ان کا اطمینان کم ہو جاتا ہے اور وہ انتخابی نتائج کو قبول کرنے میں بھی ہچکچاہٹ محسوس کرتے ہیں۔ پاکستان میں یہ صورتحال مزید پیچیدہ اس لیے ہو جاتی ہے کہ انتخابی ساکھ کا تصور رفتہ رفتہ سیاسی وابستگی سے جڑتا جا رہا ہے۔ عموماً کامیاب جماعت کے حامی انتخابات کو شفاف قرار دیتے ہیں، جبکہ شکست کھانے والی جماعت کے حامی اسی عمل پر سوال اٹھاتے ہیں۔ یہ رجحان صرف پاکستان تک محدود نہیں بلکہ دنیا کی کئی جمہوریتوں میں دیکھا گیا ہے، جسے تحقیق میں “ونر ایفیکٹ” (Winner Effect) کا نام دیا گیا ہے۔ تاہم ایک مضبوط جمہوریت کی اصل پہچان یہ ہے کہ انتخابی اداروں پر اعتماد کا انحصار اس بات پر نہ ہو کہ اقتدار کس کے حصے میں آیا ہے۔

تحقیق کا ایک اور اہم نتیجہ یہ ہے کہ انتخابی بے ضابطگی کا پہلا تجربہ یا پہلا تاثر عوامی اعتماد پر سب سے گہرا اثر ڈالتا ہے۔ جب ایک بار شکوک و شبہات جنم لے لیں تو ہر نئی انتخابی تنازعہ پہلے سے موجود بداعتمادی کو مزید مضبوط کرتا چلا جاتا ہے۔ پاکستان جیسے ملک، جہاں تقریباً ہر انتخاب کے بعد اس کی شفافیت پر مختلف بیانیے سامنے آتے ہیں، کے لیے یہ ایک سنجیدہ تنبیہ ہے۔ اعتماد ایک بار مجروح ہو جائے تو اسے بحال کرنا، اسے برقرار رکھنے سے کہیں زیادہ مشکل ہو جاتا ہے۔

اس تحقیق کا ایک بنیادی سبق یہ بھی ہے کہ صرف اداروں کی قانونی خودمختاری کافی نہیں ہوتی۔ انتخابی قوانین، آئینی ضمانتیں اور آزاد انتخابی ادارے یقیناً ضروری ہیں، لیکن عوامی اعتماد کا متبادل نہیں بن سکتے۔ شہری انتخابات کا جائزہ اس بنیاد پر لیتے ہیں کہ انتخابی عمل کتنا شفاف تھا، تمام سیاسی قوتوں کو یکساں مواقع ملے یا نہیں، نتائج بروقت سامنے آئے یا نہیں، اور قوانین کا اطلاق بلاامتیاز ہوا یا نہیں۔ کسی ادارے کی ساکھ صرف اس کے آزاد قرار دیے جانے سے قائم نہیں ہوتی بلکہ اس وقت قائم ہوتی ہے جب عوام بھی اسے حقیقتاً غیر جانبدار اور خودمختار سمجھیں۔

آئندہ عام انتخابات کی جانب بڑھتے ہوئے پاکستان کو صرف یہ بحث نہیں کرنی چاہیے کہ کون جیتے گا اور کون ہارے گا، بلکہ اصل توجہ اس بات پر ہونی چاہیے کہ انتخابی عمل پر عوام کا اعتماد کیسے مضبوط بنایا جائے۔ جمہوری استحکام صرف پُرامن انتخابات سے نہیں آتا بلکہ اس وقت ممکن ہوتا ہے جب انتخابی نتائج کو وسیع عوامی قبولیت حاصل ہو۔ یہ اعتماد اسی وقت پیدا ہو سکتا ہے جب سیاسی جماعتیں، انتخابی ادارے، عدلیہ، میڈیا اور سول سوسائٹی سب اس بات پر متفق ہوں کہ انتخابی دیانت داری کسی بھی سیاسی مفاد سے زیادہ اہم ہے۔

پاکستان کا جمہوری سفر کئی نشیب و فراز سے گزرا ہے، مگر اب اصل ضرورت جمہوری نظام کی ساکھ کو مضبوط کرنے کی ہے۔ ہر انتخاب عوام کے اعتماد میں اضافہ کرے، نہ کہ ان کے شکوک و شبہات میں۔ آئندہ انتخابات کی کامیابی کا معیار صرف ووٹر ٹرن آؤٹ یا نئی حکومت کی تشکیل نہیں ہوگا، بلکہ یہ ہوگا کہ کیا مختلف سیاسی نظریات رکھنے والے پاکستانی اس بات پر یقین رکھتے ہیں کہ انتخابی عمل شفاف، منصفانہ اور قابلِ اعتماد تھا۔
آخرکار، جمہوریت صرف انتخابات کے انعقاد سے زندہ نہیں رہتی بلکہ اس یقین سے زندہ رہتی ہے کہ ہر ووٹ کی یکساں اہمیت ہے اور ہر انتخاب حقیقی معنوں میں عوامی رائے کی عکاسی کرتا ہے۔

title: Paying the Price for Patronage: Electoral Violence in Sri Lanka
imageAlt: Electoral politics and patronage in Sri Lanka
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
paragraphs: This granular case study utilizes unique qualitative data from in-depth interviews at the village level in Sri Lanka’s Kandy District to unpack the local dynamics of endemic electoral violence. By moving beyond national-level aggregates to focus on the perspectives of victims, the authors reveal that violence is a highly instrumental tool used to suppress opposition votes and demonstrate party loyalty within a patronage-based political culture. The research identifies a critical socio-economic asymmetry in victimization: while local elites often leverage their connections to influential politicians or the security apparatus to escape harm, lower-class activists bear the brunt of physical assaults, arson, and intimidation. This violence, often outsourced to “outside thugs” to maintain local plausible deniability, has fundamentally shifted the electoral experience in rural communities from a communal “joyful” event to one characterized by lingering fear and restricted mobility.

The implications of this study are profound for understanding political behavior in developing nations like Pakistan, where the politicization of essential life opportunities creates a high-stakes environment for electoral competition. When access to jobs, contracts, and welfare is contingent upon visible political loyalty, violence becomes a rational—albeit destructive—strategy for both incumbents seeking to maintain power and challengers attempting to overcome resource asymmetries. The research suggests that state patronage serves as a catalyst for violence, as party supporters may instigate conflict to prove their utility to patrons, effectively turning the democratic process into a mechanism for resource extraction rather than representative governance. Ultimately, this environment traps citizens in “party labeling” and rigid socialization, where the cost of changing political affiliation can be physical or economic retaliation, reinforcing a cycle of political decay.

In today’s climate of persistent legitimacy crises in hybrid regimes, this work remains essential for diagnosing why institutional reforms often fail to curb violence when the underlying “politics of patronage” remains intact. As seen in contemporary South Asian electoral cycles, the erosion of public trust in the political system is often a direct result of the fear and frustration lingering years after election day. The study demonstrates that when the police and judiciary are perceived as partisan tools of the incumbent party, the resulting climate of impunity neutralizes the intended purpose of the ballot box. For the modern Pakistani context, this underscores that genuine democratic consolidation requires more than just regular elections; it necessitates the insulation of state administrative functions from partisan manipulation to protect the most vulnerable voters.

This landmark research provides a fertile starting point for fellow scholars to investigate how emerging digital platforms might disrupt—or potentially reinforce—traditional patronage networks and violent mobilization. While this study expertly maps physical violence and interpersonal fear, future scholarship should explore the intersection of digital socialization and electoral safety, specifically how online transparency and real-time monitoring might mitigate the “impunity gap” described by the authors. There is significant potential to build on this framework by conducting comparative longitudinal studies on the role of non-state actors and civil society in providing security when state institutions fail to remain neutral. By continuing to investigate these local-level dynamics, we can inspire a new generation of comparative political scientists to develop more resilient models for democratic stability that “pay a lower price” for political engagement.

title: Patterns of Socio-Political Participation in Nepal and Implications for Social Inclusion
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Haug, M., Aasland, A., & Dahal, D. R. (2009). Forum for Development Studies, 36(1), 105-136
paragraphs: This seminal study utilizes a comprehensive survey of 2,890 households across four distinct districts in Nepal to challenge long-held assumptions regarding the role of caste and ethnicity in political engagement. By constructing a sophisticated participation index, the authors categorize households into non-participants (33%), moderate participants (52%), and active participants (15%). The core findings suggest a significant departure from traditional “ethnic determinism”; instead, the research reveals that geographical location and cultural values are the primary drivers of moderate participation, while educational attainment serves as the critical gatekeeper for high-level, active political leadership. This empirical evidence indicates that a broad-based process of inclusion has taken place, where formerly marginalized groups have been mobilized into the democratic fold, effectively eroding participation gaps previously defined solely by ethnic or class hierarchies.

The broader implications for developing democracies, including Pakistan, underscore that structural mobilization can successfully bridge deep-seated socio-cultural divides even in highly stratified societies. The study demonstrates that civil society organizations and political parties have been remarkably effective in empowering the poor and marginalized to affect change from below. However, a sobering reality remains: because active participation and leadership roles are heavily correlated with human and economic resources, there is a persistent risk of continued elite dominance in positions of power. For practitioners, this suggests that simply increasing turnout is insufficient; the focus must shift toward democratizing the “active” tier of participation by making education and resources more accessible to those traditionally excluded from leadership.

In today’s volatile political climate, where many nations grapple with a “legitimacy crisis,” this research highlights the critical role of subjective perception in driving civic engagement. The authors found that a household’s subjective feeling of being excluded from the national mainstream is a more potent predictor of non-participation than their objective ethnic or religious identity. This finding is particularly relevant for the South Asian context, where political cynicism often stems from a perceived disconnect between the state and the citizen. It reinforces the idea that political participation is itself a constituent element of inclusion; the act of engaging in the process fosters a sense of national belonging that can stabilize fragile democratic systems.

This groundbreaking work invites future scholars to explore the institutional opportunity structures that vary across different regions to explain why certain locales foster higher engagement than others. While this study identifies education as a key driver of leadership, fellow researchers should investigate the specific types of “interpersonal communication” and “digital socialization” that might allow less-educated citizens to overcome traditional barriers to entry. Additionally, there is a significant need to probe how donor-funded NGOs and community-based organizations can better balance their reach between hill and plains regions to avoid creating new geographical imbalances in political agency. By building upon this rigorous multivariate framework, we can deepen our collective understanding of how to transform high levels of public activity into truly non-discriminatory and effective institutional practices.

title: Media Use and Online Political Participation: The Mediating Roles of Media Credibility and Political Trust in Jakarta and Islamabad
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Intyaswati, D., Mahmood, Q., Venus, A., Kusumajanti, & Saputra, W. T. (2025). Journal of Contemporary Eastern Asia, 24(1), 22-43
paragraphs: This rigorous comparative study utilizes Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to explore the intricate pathways through which digital political information consumption translates into online political engagement within two major South Asian and Southeast Asian capitals. By analyzing survey data from 386 residents in Islamabad and 520 in Jakarta, the authors evaluate how media credibility and political trust function as mediating variables in the digital age. A striking finding for political behaviorists is the divergence in trust dynamics: while social media use in Jakarta fosters political trust, frequent access to political information via social media in Islamabad actually reduces confidence in the government and politicians. Methodologically, the research demonstrates high academic standards by employing confirmatory factor analysis, which uniquely identified YouTube and Instagram as the primary valid sources of political information for the Islamabad cohort, while excluding platforms like TikTok and Twitter due to reliability thresholds.

The findings offer profound implications for the study of democratic consolidation in hybrid regimes, suggesting that political trust is a prerequisite for mobilizing citizens, yet the very tools used for mobilization—social media—may be eroding that trust in the Pakistani context. For researchers specializing in third-world political behavior, the study clarifies that online media consumption (websites and search engines) holds a more significant weight in fostering trust in Pakistan than in Indonesia, where social media remains the dominant trust-builder. This implies that for the Pakistani state and political actors to enhance their legitimacy, there is a dire need to shift toward objective, professional journalism and “positive political behavior” to rebuild a shattered image among a tech-savvy but cynical youth population.

In a contemporary era of hyper-polarization and economic volatility, this research is vital for understanding the “legitimacy crisis” that has gripped Pakistan since the political upheavals of early 2022. The study contextualizes its data against a backdrop of military-political shifts, high inflation, and perceptions of systemic corruption within institutions like the National Accountability Bureau (NAB). It highlights that in a climate where residents believe news channels are biased and politicians are dishonest, source credibility becomes the ultimate currency for democratic participation. This study serves as a scientific baseline to understand why certain segments of the Pakistani electorate may engage in online activism not out of trust, but as a reaction to perceived institutional failures.

This landmark comparative work provides a fertile foundation for fellow scholars to pursue longitudinal research into how digital “echo chambers” influence long-term democratic stability. Future scholarship should build upon this model by incorporating more comprehensive indicators of political trust and expanding the geographic scope beyond capital cities to capture rural-urban divides. There is a significant opportunity to explore how specific digital platforms and search engine behaviors allow citizens to bypass domestic media bias by accessing international information sources. By continuing to refine these models of digital mediation, we can better equip the academic community to predict the resilience of democratic institutions in the face of rapid technological and political disruption.

title: Major Structural Issues and Measures to Improve Political Participation of Minorities in India
imageAlt: Political participation of minorities in India
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Maidergi, V. K., & M. S., N. K. (2025). Peace Review: A Journal of Social Justice, 37(2), 293–302
paragraphs: This insightful analysis explores the systemic and procedural impediments that hinder the political agency of religious minorities in the world’s largest democracy. The authors utilize a historical and structural framework to dissect how the “First Past the Post” (FPTP) system, combined with a random delimitation of constituencies, often dilutes minority votes, leading to a “winner-take-all” outcome that strategically excludes geographically dispersed communities. Furthermore, the study identifies a shift from a pluralistic “Congress system” to a contemporary landscape dominated by hypernationalism and religious identity politics, where minority concerns are often sidelined or used as electoral rhetoric. By examining socio-economic barriers like systemic poverty and the educational disparities highlighted by the Sachar Committee, the research argues that the high material cost of political entry effectively disenfranchises those struggling for basic survival.

The evidence presented underscores a critical need for structural reform that transcends simple electoral cycles, offering a blueprint for more inclusive governance in diverse South Asian contexts like Pakistan. The authors suggest that moving toward a hybrid system that integrates proportional representation in minority-concentrated areas could transform “wasted votes” into meaningful political capital. For political parties, the transition toward internal democratic norms—such as transparent candidate selection and institutionalized quotas—is not merely an ethical imperative but a strategic necessity to foster cross-communal solidarity. These findings imply that the health of a democratic republic is fundamentally tied to its ability to provide a non-discriminatory distribution of political goods and leadership opportunities for its most vulnerable populations.

In the current global climate of rising populism and right-wing assertion, this study provides a timely scientific lens through which to view the “legitimacy crisis” facing modern multi-ethnic states. The resilience of the Indian electorate in recent elections serves as a poignant reminder that there are checks on “strongmanship” and that public appetite for pluralistic representation remains high. This research is particularly relevant for contemporary activists and scholars following movements like the anti-CAA protests, as it demonstrates how “social solidarity” can stall exclusionary legislation and force a re-evaluation of the state’s relationship with its minorities. It highlights that without a clear, constitutional definition of what constitutes a “minority,” these groups remain prone to political exploitation and administrative neglect.

This comprehensive review serves as a catalyst for future researchers to delve deeper into the intersection of digital mobilization and minority political agency in the Global South. Future scholarship could build on this foundation by examining how the “digital divide” interacts with the socio-economic barriers identified here, or how the judiciary influences the security of minority voters during contentious periods. There is also significant potential to explore the “wisdom of the crowds” through comparative analyses of grassroots solidarity movements across South Asian borders. By refining our understanding of these structural bottlenecks, we can inspire a new generation of comparative politics scholars to design frameworks that move beyond competitive exclusion toward a more collaborative and truly representative democratic future.

title: Influence of Political Socialization Agents on Pakistani Youth’s Political Participation: The Mediating Role of Media and Interpersonal Communication.
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Memon, S., Ishak, M. S., & Hamid, N. A. (2018). Jurnal Komunikasi Malaysian Journal of Communication, 34(2), 121-136
paragraphs: This rigorous investigation utilizes Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to map the complex pathways through which Pakistani university students are socialized into democratic life. By surveying 228 social science students, the authors move beyond traditional “fixed functionalism”—which emphasizes the mere acquisition of system-maintaining norms—to explore how youth develop the actual capacities for meaningful participation. A primary finding of this research is the overwhelming dominance of peer norms over the family unit in driving both media consumption and political behavior. While a concept-oriented family environment (one that encourages open discussion) successfully prompts youth to seek out news, it does not directly translate into political action. Instead, it is the “media surveillance norms” and social pressure within peer groups that effectively foster the skills and motivations necessary for active engagement.

The findings provide a sophisticated empirical justification for the “communication mediation model,” demonstrating that informational media does not act as a “magic bullet” but requires the bridge of interpersonal deliberation to spark action. This suggests that for political participation to take root in the Global South, the mere availability of information through TV or newspapers is insufficient; it must be processed through “interpersonal communication,” including both face-to-face talk and online messaging. For practitioners in Pakistan, these implications are vital: democratic reform must focus on creating “domestic public spheres” and encouraging peer-led volunteering or scaffolding programs that move youth from passive news consumption to active expression.

In an era where the “apathetic youth” narrative often dominates political discourse, this study is critically relevant for addressing the persistent legitimacy crisis and low voter turnout in Pakistan. With nearly 45 percent of the Pakistani citizenry remaining inactive in the governing process, understanding that youth respond more to peer-mediated social capital than to traditional top-down socialization is essential for any mobilization strategy. The research highlights that the digital transition has not erased the need for human connection; rather, online messaging now serves as a modern mediator that gives youth the confidence and “talking points” necessary to enter the real-life arena of political contention.

This landmark study serves as a foundational call for fellow researchers to further explore the “dosage versus potency” of digital socialization agents in increasingly polarized environments. Future scholarship should build upon this model by investigating how regional differences—such as the rural-urban divide—might alter the influence of these socialization agents, particularly as individuals age and their dependency on family versus peers shifts. There is also immense potential to explore how specific types of interpersonal communication, such as deliberative versus conflictual talk, affect the long-term stability of democratic values. By continuing this line of rigorous empirical inquiry, we can better understand how to empower the next generation of Pakistani citizens to move from the digital sidelines to the heart of the democratic process.

title: Effects of sociodemographic variables and Facebook group membership on students political participation
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Mahmood, Q. K., Bhutta, M. H., & ul Haq, M. A. (2018). Education and Information Technologies, 23, 2235–2247
paragraphs: The study provides a rigorous empirical analysis of how the information society is reshaping the political landscape for Pakistan’s youth, utilizing a robust cross-sectional survey of 1,245 university students in Lahore. By employing exploratory factor analysis and inferential statistics, the authors demonstrate that while youth have often been characterized as politically indifferent, they are increasingly engaged in “innovative” political acts, showing a significantly higher inclination toward online participation via Facebook than traditional offline activities. The data reveals that sociodemographic factors—specifically gender, residency status, and educational attainment—play a decisive role in participation levels, with postgraduate students and male respondents consistently exhibiting higher levels of engagement in both digital and physical political spheres. Central to the research is the transformative power of digital affiliation; membership in Facebook groups, particularly those tied to political parties, serves as a potent catalyst that significantly boosts a student’s likelihood of engaging in both online discourse and offline mobilization.

These findings suggest a paradigm shift in how we conceptualize democratic “lubricants” in developing nations, moving away from traditional metrics of participation toward digitally-mediated civic engagement. For the political landscape of Pakistan, the research implies that political parties can no longer rely solely on physical infrastructure but must cultivate sophisticated digital ecosystems to capture the interest of a youth population that increasingly uses social media to bypass traditional informational barriers. Furthermore, the study highlights that digital empowerment is not inherently egalitarian; the persistent gendered and educational disparities in participation suggest that without institutional reform, the digital divide may inadvertently reinforce existing social hierarchies in the Global South.

In a contemporary political climate defined by the rapid digitalization of the public sphere, this research remains acutely relevant as it addresses the “legitimacy gap” between a traditional political class and a tech-savvy generation. As Pakistan’s social media population continues to grow, the ability to mobilize educated youth through targeted Facebook group membership has become a defining feature of modern political movements and electioneering. This study provides the scientific evidence needed to understand why contemporary youth-led movements are increasingly effective: they leverage online platforms to transform individual grievances into collective “connective action” that exerts real-world political pressure.

This landmark investigation serves as a vital call to action for the academic community to move beyond binary views of technology and instead explore the nuanced psychological and environmental factors that drive political efficacy. Future scholarship should build upon this framework by investigating the role of personality traits, political orientation, and the impact of the broader political environment on how online interactions translate into sustained democratic stability. There is immense potential for researchers to conduct longitudinal studies that track how the “wisdom of the crowds” on digital platforms influences actual policy outcomes and the long-term consolidation of democracy in the region.

title: Digital citizen empowerment: A systematic literature review of theories and development models
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Sharma, S., Kar, A. K., Gupta, M. P., Dwivedi, Y. K., & Janssen, M. (2022). Information Technology for Development, 28(4), 660–687
paragraphs: This sophisticated systematic literature review synthesizes two decades of interdisciplinary research to chart the evolution of Digital Citizen Empowerment (DCE), a process that transforms individuals from passive users into civic solution innovators. By analyzing 72 core articles from the Scopus and Web of Science databases, the authors identify four thematic strategies that define the state-citizen relationship: Multi-channel Service Delivery (MCSD), Participatory Budgeting (PB), Deliberative Governance (DG), and Digital Activism (DA). The study argues that the world has shifted from traditional New Public Management toward Digital-Era Governance (DEG), which focuses on reintegrating administrative infrastructure to provide holistic, collaborative services that empower the marginalized. Crucially, the authors present a four-stage conceptual model for the phase-wise development of information societies, moving from basic ICT infrastructure to a digitally connected ecosystem characterized by sustainable socio-political participation and social accountability.

For developing nations like Pakistan, where democratic consolidation is often hindered by elite capture and the digital divide, these findings offer a vital framework for institutional reform. The research highlights that ICT can serve as a “leveler” for social barriers, provided that governance shifts toward a citizen-centric capability development approach rather than a top-down technocratic one. For the Pakistani context, the transition toward deliberative platforms—where policy decisions are based on shared learning and consensus-building—could mitigate the “legitimacy crisis” by fostering trust between the state and its citizens. The study’s emphasis on social accountability (demand-side) provides a roadmap for civil society organizations to hold government officials responsible, ensuring that digital services translate into tangible public value rather than reinforced managerialism.

In a contemporary political climate defined by the rapid digitalization of the public sphere, this study addresses the urgent need to balance state power with active citizen intervention. The research is particularly relevant today as governments worldwide invest in smart cities, where the credibility of decisions increasingly depends on the quality and sustained engagement of the citizenry. For the modern youth, digital platforms have become a primary space for political discourse; this study explains how these interactions can be harnessed for connective action to evaluate government performance and combat corruption. It serves as a scientific warning that unless digital initiatives are designed with policy-coherent sustainability, they risk creating “surveillance societies” that worsen the digital activism gap among vulnerable populations.

This pioneering systematic review provides a robust foundation for fellow scholars to explore the psychological and structural determinants of political participation in the digital age. Future research should build upon this model by investigating the role of behavioral strategies in promoting high-quality civic engagement and examining how the triadic model of State-Citizen-Service Providers affects the flow of accountability. There is immense potential to explore the “wisdom of the crowds” through crowdsensing to monitor local administration and enforce transparency in volatile democratic environments. By continuing to investigate these four strategic streams, the academic community can inspire a new generation of researchers to bridge the gap between technological deployment and the actualization of human dignity in our global information societies.

title: Analysis of determinants of voter turnout in Indian states for election years 1991–2019
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Menon, S. M., & Rassendren, G. (2022). Journal of Social and Economic Development, 24, 30–45
paragraphs: This sophisticated longitudinal study utilizes panel regression and fixed effect models to dissect the economic underpinnings of electoral participation in the world’s largest democracy. Grounded in Rational Choice Theory, the authors examine how economic forces—specifically per-capita income, employment, and even climatic variables like monsoon patterns—influence the utility a voter derives from the ballot. A central and provocative finding is the identified “educated apathy” paradox: higher literacy rates and urbanization do not consistently correlate with higher turnout; in fact, increased literacy was associated with a slight reduction in participation across some models. This suggests that as cognitive ability and information access increase, so too may political cynicism or the perceived opportunity cost of voting, a significant departure from traditional modernization theories.

The evidence presented offers profound insights for the broader South Asian context, particularly for Pakistan, where structural barriers and economic shocks similarly dictate political life. The positive correlation between employment, income, and turnout suggests that a stable middle class is a prerequisite for a vibrant, participatory democracy. For a nation like Pakistan, which frequently grapples with high inflation and income inequality, these findings imply that voter disenfranchisement is often a rational response to economic adversity rather than a simple lack of civic awareness. The study underscores that “free and fair” elections require more than just ballot integrity; they require a socio-economic environment where the sovereignty of the voter is backed by tangible material security.

In an era where developing democracies are facing a persistent legitimacy crisis, understanding the drivers of voter abstention is more critical than ever. The research highlights that systemic issues such as bureaucratic loopholes, corruption, and inefficient governance are potent deterrents that can neutralize the “festivity” of the electoral process. As Pakistan navigates its own complex political transitions, this study serves as a vital reminder that the legitimacy of a democratic system is inextricably linked to its ability to provide economic utility to its citizens. It challenges the notion that low turnout is merely a sign of regional backwardness, revealing instead that it is often a symptom of a governance gap that transcends literacy.

This rigorous framework provides an excellent template for future scholars to investigate the nuanced interplay between digital mobilization and traditional economic determinants. While this study expertly maps the impact of physical monsoons on voter revenue and participation, subsequent research could explore “digital monsoons”—the deluge of social media information and its effect on the perceived utility of voting in developing nations. There is significant potential to expand this methodology to include the role of the judiciary and the military in shaping voter confidence. By continuing to build upon this empirical foundation, fellow researchers can deepen our collective understanding of South Asian political behavior, ensuring our democratic theories remain as dynamic and resilient as the populations they represent.

title: A scientific approach to measure public political participation in Pakistan
author: Dr. Adil Zaman
citation: Mangi, S. N., Shah, N., & Soomro, B. A. (2019). Asian Journal of Political Science, 27(1), 88–107
paragraphs: The study provides a rigorous quantitative investigation into why Pakistan ranks 164th globally in voter turnout, utilizing a robust nationwide sample of 1,884 respondents. By employing confirmatory factor analysis and stepwise hierarchical regression, the authors systematically evaluate five critical determinants of political participation: democratic party structures, party mobilization, security, accessibility, and leadership image. The data confirms that while all five factors significantly drive participation, the political landscape is heavily marred by feudalism and dynasticism, where parties often function to protect elite interests rather than represent the populace. Crucially, the research identifies citizen distrust as a potent negative moderator that dampens the positive effects of these variables, highlighting a profound psychological and structural disconnect between the state and its citizens.

These findings suggest that the path to a consolidated democracy in Pakistan requires more than just regular electoral cycles; it demands the fundamental reform of political parties into truly democratic institutions. For practitioners and policymakers, this research emphasizes that enhancing security and ballot box accessibility—specifically through non-traditional venues like shopping malls or mobile polling stations in remote areas—is vital to capturing disenfranchised voters. On a theoretical level, the study demonstrates that political mobilization and empowerment are far more critical than general education alone in fostering a participatory culture. The evidence indicates that unless parties provide equal opportunities to the middle and lower classes, the legitimacy of the entire democratic system will remain precarious.

In the current political climate, characterized by frequent protests and persistent demands for regime change, this study remains highly relevant by addressing the root causes of low legitimacy and public apathy. The “legitimacy crisis” observed in Pakistan stems from a system where over half the population does not feel it is their duty to vote, a sentiment exacerbated by perceived bad governance, income inequality, and political cynicism. This research offers a scientific framework to understand these grievances, proving that high levels of citizen distrust can neutralize even the most active mobilization efforts or charismatic leadership. It underscores that the contemporary demand for technocratic alternatives is a direct symptom of the failure of traditional party structures to inspire public trust.

This pioneering work opens numerous avenues for fellow scholars to further probe the fragile electoral dynamics of developing nations. Future research should aim to explore the specific roles of the judiciary and the military in shaping political behavior, as well as the impact of regionalism and public apathy on long-term democratic stability. There is also a significant need to investigate how electronic and social media can be leveraged to increase transparency and bridge the trust gap in the electoral process. By building upon this scientific foundation, we can collectively deepen our understanding of how to empower citizens and ensure that the “tilled land” of democracy finally yields a representative and stable harvest in Pakistan
